title: Integrated wastewater and clinical genomic surveillance for high-resolution tracking of measles virus evolution and transmission - Nature Medicine
byline: Gwala; Sipho; Levy; Joshua I; Mabasa; Victor; Subramoney; Kathleen; Ndlovu; Nkosenhle L; Kent; Chris; Jeshvaghane; Maryam Ahmadi; Gangavarapu; Praneeth; Sikakan
html:
Abstract

Measles outbreaks have surged globally, challenging surveillance and control efforts. In South Africa, the 2024−2025 measles outbreak led to nearly 4,000 reported cases, triggering a nationwide vaccination campaign. However, tracking measles virus (MeV; species Morbillivirus hominis) transmission and evolution remains difficult at scale, particularly in settings with limited access to care, diagnostic testing and sequencing capacity. Wastewater can enable population-scale virus surveillance, but low MeV concentrations limit detection sensitivity and sequencing quality. Here we show that overcoming these technical challenges enables integrated wastewater and clinical genomic surveillance that expands the coverage and resolution of MeV monitoring. We developed a virus concentration and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) workflow and applied it to 4,502 wastewater samples collected across all nine provinces of South Africa during the 2024−2025 outbreak. Wastewater MeV genotype prevalence tracked clinical estimates, and phylogenetic analyses combining wastewater and clinical sequences revealed geographically structured transmission and previously undetected inter-provincial spread. WGS recovered transmission links not captured by the field standard approach, which targets a 450-nucleotide region of the nucleoprotein gene (N450), highlighting the importance of WGS to accurately characterize transmission dynamics. Our study provides a cost-effective and scalable genomic surveillance approach to support measles control and elimination.

Main

Measles, caused by MeV (species M. hominis), is among the most contagious diseases, requiring more than 95% vaccination coverage for herd-based immunity1. Despite major reduction in global incidence after public vaccine introduction in 1963 (ref. 2), outbreaks have resurged after decreases in vaccination coverage3,4 due to ongoing health system weaknesses, vaccine hesitancy, disinformation and the COVID-19 pandemic5,6,7. Surveillance programs that identify areas of MeV transmission and immunity gaps8 are, therefore, critical to achieve the World Health Organization (WHO) Measles and Rubella Strategic Framework 2021−2030 vision of ‘a world free from measles and rubella’9. Meeting this goal will require surveillance strategies that are more comprehensive and sustainable and build upon existing measles programmatic surveillance tools, including case-based surveillance, contact tracing and quarantine and genome sequencing. Scalable approaches are required in both resource-rich and resource-limited contexts to provide timely, sensitive and reliable data to inform public health responses.

During an infection, MeV is shed through respiratory secretions, oral fluids and urine10,11,12,13,14 and can be detected downstream in wastewater15,16,17,18,19. As demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic17,20,21,22, wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) can provide population-level insights into pathogen transmission with reduced sampling bias and serve as a valuable complement to clinical monitoring. Although WES has been shown to enable detection of wild-type MeV15,17,23,24,25,26, its use in MeV genomic surveillance remains limited. Genome sequencing of MeV in wastewater may improve tracking of genotype prevalence, help demonstrate chains of transmission and identify new outbreaks15,27,28.

Programmatic MeV sequencing conducted under Global Measles and Rubella Laboratory Network (GMRLN) guidelines targets a 450-nucleotide region at the 3′ end of the nucleoprotein gene (N450)29,30,31. Selected in 1998, when there were more than 18 circulating MeV genotypes, the N450 region covers less than 3% of the 15.9-kb MeV genome and was designed to support genotype assignment and basic tracking of transmission pathways29,32. However, increased vaccination coverage and decreased measles transmission over the period 2000−2020 led to the elimination of all but two circulating measles genotypes, B3 and D8 (ref. 29). As a result, N450 sequences do not provide sufficient resolution to track virus transmission33,34, making it difficult to differentiate between local and imported strains29. Recent advances in virus concentration, combined with tiled amplicon scheme design35, now enable low-cost WGS, including from wastewater samples with low viral loads and fragmented RNA35,36.

In South Africa, measles-containing vaccine (MCV) is administered through the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI-SA) at 6 months and 12 months of age37, with supplementary mass immunization activities conducted every 3−4 years38. Vaccination coverage remains below the 95% herd immunity threshold39, and measles outbreaks occur intermittently40. Since August 2024, measles outbreaks have led to 931 and 2,756 laboratory-confirmed cases in 2024 (ref. 41) and 2025 (ref. 42), respectively. These outbreaks coincided with a national rubella outbreak, beginning in late July (epidemiological week 31) 2024 and declining by 31 December 2024 (ref. 43), leading to a supplementary immunization activity in June−August 2025. Measles and rubella surveillance depends on clinicians to report fever-rash cases and submit serum specimens for simultaneous testing for measles and rubella immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies. If urine or throat swabs are submitted and laboratory capacity allows, these specimens undergo polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and N450 sequencing following GMRLN guidelines. Both genotypes B3 and D8 have been detected in clusters of cases or outbreaks since 2021, and sequences are regularly submitted to the Measles Nucleotide Surveillance (MeaNS) database44.

In the present study, using combined wastewater and clinical MeV WES, we demonstrate that wastewater-based MeV surveillance expands outbreak tracking and improves characterization of MeV spread and evolution. Through longitudinal multimodal virus detection and sequencing across South Africa during concurrent measles and rubella outbreaks, we show that wastewater MeV surveillance closely tracks laboratory-confirmed fever-rash cases and reveals wild-type virus spread not captured by available clinical surveillance. Wastewater-derived genomes cluster with clinical sequences from South Africa and identify transmission links and virus diversity that cannot be resolved using N450 sequencing. Together, these results establish wastewater genomic surveillance as a scalable approach for high-resolution monitoring of measles transmission and support its use in measles elimination efforts, including in resource-limited settings.

Results

Wastewater surveillance tracks community MeV burden over time

The 2024−2025 measles outbreak in South Africa affected all nine provinces, with over 50% of laboratory-confirmed cases reported in Gauteng Province45 (Fig. 1a). To supplement fever-rash surveillance for measles, we previously expanded the South African national WES program to include MeV detection in week 10 of 2024 (ref. 17). To further improve MeV wastewater detection sensitivity, we compared effectiveness of new two virus concentration approaches—a single magnetic capture bead method (Dynabeads; method A) and a two-bead method (Dynabeads and Ceres Nanotrap; method B)—with our initial method, centrifugal ultrafiltration (Centricon; method C) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Although all three methods yielded similar viral loads on average (Extended Data Fig. 1b), method A was the most time- and cost-effective option (Supplementary Table 1). Therefore, from week 41 of 2024, method C was replaced by method A for routine processing of wastewater samples.

The line represents the best-fit linear regression (R2 = 0.76), and the gray shaded band represents the bootstrap 95% CI of the fitted regression. d, Aggregate national clinical positive cases as determined by IgM serological testing (red dashed line) and clinical TPR (light red line) per epiweek from January 2024 through August 2025, smoothed with a rolling average of width 2 epiweeks (top). From 1 January 2024 to 31 August 2025, we collected and analyzed 4,502 wastewater samples from 14 health districts across South Africa (Extended Data Fig. 2a). All collected wastewater samples were tested for MeV using reverse transcription digital polymerase chain reaction (RT−dPCR). We found that 395 samples (8.8%) were positive for MeV RNA. Wastewater test positivity rate (TPR) was highest in Johannesburg district (69/568, 12.1%), consistent with case reporting (Fig. 1b). Although we observed no detections in two districts with very low numbers of wastewater samples collected (n = 21,24), wastewater TPR in all other districts ranged between 3.9% and 9.4%. Overall, we found that the wastewater TPR for each district was strongly correlated with the number of observed cases (Spearman’s ρ = 0.89, P = 8.4 × 10−5; Fig. 1c).

Wastewater sample counts were largely consistent over time (Extended Data Fig. 2a), but clinical testing volume varied substantially, increasing from a baseline of approximately 100 samples per week to more than 1,000 per week between September and December 2024 on account of rubella outbreak surveillance efforts (Extended Data Fig. 2b). As a result of the large volume of specimens submitted for rubella testing, measles clinical TPR remained low during 2024, despite substantial increases in both laboratory-confirmed measles cases and wastewater TPR (Fig. 1d). During the rubella outbreak, demand for fever-rash laboratory testing exceeded what available personnel and testing resources could process, likely limiting clinical measles case ascertainment rates and potentially leading to underestimation of measles burden, despite an overall increase in testing volume.

Comparing national wastewater TPR with clinical test results over time, we found that the number of clinical test positives and wastewater TPR were weakly correlated (Pearson’s r = 0.32, P = 2.7 × 10−3; Extended Data Fig. 2c), but clinical TPR and wastewater TPR were not correlated (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Additionally, we found that wastewater surveillance suggested an increase in TPR preceding the increase in measles cases in August−October 2024, although wastewater viral load did not increase until September 2024. To investigate the relationship between wastewater and clinical surveillance at greater spatial resolution, we performed focused analyses on Gauteng districts, which had the most frequent wastewater sampling (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We found significant correlations between wastewater TPR and clinical test positives in both City of Johannesburg (Spearman’s ρ = 0.65, P = 0.002; Extended Data Fig. 3b) and City of Tshwane (Spearman’s ρ = 0.51, P = 0.021; Extended Data Fig. 3c) but not in Ekurhuleni (Extended Data Fig. 3d). These results indicated that wastewater TPR generally correlated with clinical test positives and that concordance may be influenced by wastewater surveillance coverage and clinical reporting differences across districts.

To characterize the temporal relationship between wastewater and clinical signals, we performed a lead-lag analysis between wastewater TPR and clinical test positives at national scale (Extended Data Fig. 4). We observed maximum cross-correlation at a lag corresponding to wastewater TPR preceding clinical case counts by 1 week. However, cross-correlation at zero temporal shift and several clinical leading shifts were similar in magnitude, preventing identification of a specific temporal offset between the signals.

Whole-genome wastewater sequencing recovers longitudinal genotype prevalence

Although clinical N450 sequencing volume increased in 2024 and 2025 relative to previous years, only 6.8% of laboratory-confirmed IgM-positive samples were sequenced, and uneven availability of sample collection and transport may limit the utility of genomic data to support outbreak response (Fig. 2a). To supplement tracking of MeV genotype prevalence using wastewater, we implemented a combined virus concentration and amplicon sequencing approach starting in October 2024 (ref. 35) (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). We attempted to sequence all wastewater samples that were MeV positive via RT−dPCR, including samples at the assay limit of detection, corresponding to a single positive partition, as low as 0.346 genome copies per microliter. We found that genome coverage increased with measured viral concentration across wastewater samples, with an empirical relationship consistent with improved recovery at higher viral loads (Extended Data Fig. 5c and Supplementary Table 2). However, this relationship should not be interpreted as a formal correlation analysis, as wastewater matrix effects, including residual RT and PCR inhibitors, can influence copy-to-coverage relationships.

a, Counts of MeV sequences from 2022 to 2025 by year, separated by genotype, in South Africa. b, Estimated measles genotype composition for each wastewater sample using Freyja, across all sequenced samples. ‘B3’ and ‘D8’ indicate samples with estimated 100% composition of that genotype. ‘B3&D8’ indicates that multiple genotypes are present in the sample. c, For the period 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025, quarterly clinical (solid bars) and wastewater (dotted bars) MeV genotype prevalence. Numbers of clinical and wastewater samples per quarter are indicated in parentheses. d, Overall genotype prevalence for each national WWTP surveillance site in Gauteng Province. e, Overall genotype prevalence at each sub-catchment sampling site. Boundary data are from the Humanitarian Data Exchange (https://data.humdata.org/dataset/cod-ab-zaf).

To estimate MeV genotype prevalence from virus mixtures, we extended our Freyja bioinformatic tool46 to incorporate available MeV genomes and cladistic nomenclature into genotype-defining mutation barcodes47. To test this sequencing and analysis workflow, we first identified potential amplicon primer failures across all available whole-genome sequences (Extended Data Fig. 6a) and used representative sequences to simulate amplicon sequencing of genotype mixtures and analyze genotype prevalence recovery (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c). We found that our approach accurately recovered genotype prevalence for all reference samples, including those with potential amplicon primer failure (R2 = 0.99). To further validate our approach, we performed WGS of both vaccine strain (genotype A) MeV and clinical specimens from genotypes B3 and D8. In each case, Freyja correctly assigned samples to their expected genotypes based on N450 sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e). These results indicated that Freyja accurately recovered MeV genotype prevalence estimates for pure and mixed genotype samples in both simulated and real sequencing tests, respectively, similar to previous results for SARS-CoV-2, MPXV and ZIKV36,46.

To evaluate performance with real-world wastewater samples and compare results with clinical surveillance, we analyzed all available wastewater sequence data. Of the 395 samples that tested positive, 91 (23.0%) were successfully amplified and sequenced, of which 69 had sufficient coverage to recover genotype prevalence estimates. Among these, 68 samples contained only one genotype (40 B3 and 28 D8), and one sample contained both B3 and D8 (Fig. 2b). We did not identify any samples with genotype A, indicating that MeV detected in wastewater derived from wild-type infections rather than vaccine-derived shedding.
